title: Data Compression Cuts I/O
description: An uncompressed table reads far more pages than needed for a scan; PAGE compression shrinks it and cuts the I/O. Why it matters: page compression is a low-effort, high-value lever for I/O-bound tables that many teams never enable simply because they don't know the tradeoffs.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Every table in SQL Server is stored as a stack of fixed-size 8KB pages, and the cost of reading a table is measured mainly in how many of those pages have to be pulled off disk (or, if you're lucky, found already sitting in memory). If you can fit more rows onto each page, you need fewer pages to hold the same table, and every scan, seek, or range read touches fewer pages — meaning less I/O, faster queries, and a smaller memory footprint for caching the same amount of data. That's the entire idea behind SQL Server's built-in **data compression** feature: shrink how much physical space each row takes up, so more of the table's actual information fits into the same 8KB pages.

There are two levels: **ROW** compression, which stores each value more efficiently on its own — for example, storing a small integer like `5` using only one byte instead of the full four bytes an `INT` column normally reserves, and simply omitting storage for fixed-length columns that happen to be NULL or zero. Then there's **PAGE** compression, which builds on top of row compression and adds two cleverer tricks that operate across a whole page at once. **Prefix compression** looks at a column's values across all the rows on a page and, if they share a common leading prefix (e.g., many customer codes starting with 'CUST-'), stores that shared prefix once and only the differing remainder per row. **Dictionary compression** goes further: it scans the *entire page* for any repeated values, anywhere in any column, builds a small lookup table of those repeated values, and replaces every occurrence with a short reference to the dictionary entry instead of storing the same bytes over and over.

This is where the specific setup in this lesson matters: PAGE compression is spectacularly effective on columns that are **low-cardinality** (few distinct values) and repetitive. Picture a `Status` column that can only ever be one of three values ('Pending', 'Shipped', 'Cancelled') repeated across 500,000 rows, or a `Region` column stored as a fixed-width `CHAR(20)` — meaning every single value is padded out to a full 20 bytes even though the real region name might only be 6 or 7 characters, with only 4 distinct region values total across the whole table. A page holding a chunk of that data is, from a compression algorithm's point of view, wildly redundant: the same handful of strings repeated hundreds of times per page. Dictionary compression collapses all those repeats down to tiny references, and the padded `CHAR(20)` waste disappears along with it. The practical result: dramatically more rows fit per 8KB page than before.

Why does this actually speed up queries, rather than just save disk space? Because a scan's cost in SQL Server is measured in **logical reads** — essentially, 'how many 8KB pages did I have to touch to answer this query.' If compression lets twice as many rows fit on each page, then a full scan of the table needs roughly half as many logical reads to see every row, whether that data comes off disk or out of the buffer pool cache in memory. Fewer pages to walk through means the scan finishes faster and puts less pressure on the buffer pool (SQL Server's in-memory cache of pages), which in turn means more of your *other* frequently used tables can stay cached in memory rather than getting evicted to make room. The tradeoff, and it's a real one, is CPU: every time a compressed page is read, SQL Server has to spend a small amount of extra CPU work decompressing it back into a usable row format before it can process the data. For most read-heavy, I/O-bound workloads — which describes the vast majority of reporting and dashboard-style queries — that CPU cost is small compared to the I/O savings, making compression a straightforward net win.

Why is this a lever many teams never pull, even when it would clearly help? Partly because it requires an explicit `ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = ...)` — it's opt-in, not automatic, and rebuilding an index (especially on a huge production table) is an operation people are often (rightly) cautious about scheduling. Partly because the tradeoff (a little more CPU for a lot less I/O) sounds intimidating without evidence, so teams leave well enough alone rather than risk unknown CPU regressions. SQL Server actually ships a built-in tool to remove the guesswork here: `sys.sp_estimate_data_compression_savings`, a system stored procedure that can tell you, *before* you commit to anything, roughly how much smaller a table would become under ROW versus PAGE compression, without actually rebuilding it. Once compressed, a scan that used to plow through thousands of pages of padded, repetitive data can drop to a small fraction of that page count, purely because more real rows now fit in each 8KB unit — no query rewrite required, no index redesign, just a smarter physical layout for the same data.

## Scenario
A 500,000-row `Orders` table is scanned constantly by reports. Many columns are low-cardinality and repetitive (`Status` has 3 values, `Region` is a padded `CHAR(20)` with 4 values). A simple `SELECT COUNT(*)` reads thousands of pages.

## The idea
**Data compression** (`ROW` or `PAGE`) stores more rows per page. `PAGE` compression adds per-page **prefix** and **dictionary** encoding, which is extremely effective on repetitive columns. Fewer pages means every scan and range read performs **fewer logical reads** — a pure I/O win, paid for with a little CPU to decompress.

## What to look for
- Before: a **Clustered Index Scan** reading the full (uncompressed) page count.
- After a `REBUILD ... WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE)`: the same scan reads far fewer pages.
- Estimate the savings first with `sys.sp_estimate_data_compression_savings`.

## The fix
`ALTER INDEX PK_Orders ON Orders REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE);` then re-run the scan. (Compression trades CPU for I/O, so it shines on read-heavy, scan-heavy, compressible tables.)
hints: COUNT(*) scans the clustered index. Its cost is the number of PAGES, not rows -- how could we fit more rows per page?
Region (CHAR(20), 4 values) and Status (3 values) are highly repetitive -- ideal for PAGE dictionary/prefix compression.
ALTER INDEX PK_Orders ON Orders REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE); then re-run SELECT COUNT(*).
